questions.question: What are the differences between HashMap, TreeMap, and LinkedHashMap?
questions.title: Map Implementations Comparison
questions.direct_answer: **`HashMap`** gives **O(1)** average lookup with **no ordering**. **`LinkedHashMap`** keeps **insertion (or access) order** at O(1) by adding a linked list. **`TreeMap`** keeps keys **sorted** (natural or `Comparator`) using a red-black tree, at **O(log n)**.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of Map implementation trade-offs and when to choose each based on ordering and performance requirements
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Confusing LinkedHashMap's insertion-order preservation with TreeMap's sorted order, or thinking all Maps have the same performance characteristics
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention LinkedHashMap's access-order mode for LRU caches and TreeMap's NavigableMap interface for range queries

sections.title: Three Map Flavors for Different Needs
sections.content:
A **`Map`** stores data as **key-value pairs** — you give it a key, it gives back a value. `HashMap`, `LinkedHashMap`, and `TreeMap` are the three `Map` classes you reach for most. They store the same pairs, but they differ in **iteration order** and **speed**.

**`HashMap`** is the **default**. It uses a hash table, so `get` and `put` run in **O(1)** on average. The price is **no order** — iterate it and entries come out in no predictable sequence.

**`LinkedHashMap`** is a `HashMap` that **remembers order**. It adds a doubly-linked list through the entries, so iteration follows the order you inserted them. Same `O(1)` speed, a little more memory. Switch on **access-order mode** and it moves touched entries to the end — the foundation of an **LRU cache**.

**`TreeMap`** keeps keys **sorted**. It stores them in a **red-black tree** (a self-balancing binary search tree), so `get` and `put` cost **O(log n)**. In return you get sorted iteration and **range queries** through the `NavigableMap` interface.

Think of three filing systems: `HashMap` is a messy drawer where any file is instant, `LinkedHashMap` keeps files in the order you filed them, and `TreeMap` keeps them alphabetised.

> **The rule:** ordering and sorting cost you speed. Reach for `HashMap` first; move to `LinkedHashMap` for insertion order or `TreeMap` for sorted keys.

sections.title: Map Implementations at a Glance
sections.content:
emerald|HashMap|~Hash table, no order|O(1) get/put|one null key allowed|the fast default
blue|LinkedHashMap|~HashMap + linked list|O(1) get/put|insertion or access order|access-order = LRU cache
violet|TreeMap|~Red-black tree|O(log n) get/put|sorted by key, no null key|NavigableMap range queries
amber|Pick by need|~Order vs speed|no order -> HashMap|remember order -> LinkedHashMap|sorted/ranges -> TreeMap

sections.title: Pick a Map by the Behaviour You Need
sections.content:
One question — do you care about order? — picks the class for almost every real case. ```mermaid flowchart TD Q["Need a Map?"] --> O{"Care about order?"} O -->|"No"| H["HashMap
O(1), no order"] O -->|"Insertion order"| L["LinkedHashMap
O(1), keeps order"] O -->|"Sorted keys"| T["TreeMap
O(log n), sorted"] L --> LRU["access-order mode
powers an LRU cache"] T --> R["NavigableMap
range queries"] ``` Start at the top, and the ordering choice walks you straight to the right class.

sections.title: HashMap when iteration order actually matters
Match the Map to the ordering requirement
When to Choose Each Map
sections.content:
Use **`HashMap`** when you need fast key-value lookups and don't care about iteration order — caching user sessions by sessionId, or storing product prices by SKU.

Use **`LinkedHashMap`** when you need predictable iteration order, like rendering form fields in the order they were added, or when building an **LRU cache** with access-order mode.

Use **`TreeMap`** when you need sorted keys for **range queries** — all orders between two timestamps, or products inside a price range. It's also handy when you want sorted iteration without re-sorting a list every time.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Confusing insertion order with sorted order:** freshers think `LinkedHashMap` sorts entries, but it only preserves the order you put them in — `TreeMap` is the one that sorts.
- **Using TreeMap for simple lookups:** choosing `TreeMap` when you don't need sorting wastes memory and speed — `O(log n)` is slower than `HashMap`'s `O(1)` for plain get/put.
- **Forgetting null key restrictions:** a null key in `TreeMap` throws `NullPointerException` during comparison, while `HashMap` and `LinkedHashMap` allow one null key.
- **Assuming HashMap order is stable:** the order can even change across resizes, so never rely on it for output.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **`HashMap`** — fastest option with `O(1)` operations, but no iteration-order guarantee.
**`LinkedHashMap`** — extends `HashMap`, adding insertion-order or access-order via a doubly-linked list.
**`TreeMap`** — implements `NavigableMap` over a red-black tree for `O(log n)` operations with sorted keys.
**Access-order mode** — `LinkedHashMap` with `accessOrder=true` moves entries to the end on `get`, the basis of LRU caches.
**Null keys** — `HashMap` and `LinkedHashMap` allow one null key; `TreeMap` throws on null keys.
**Pick by need** — fast lookup goes to `HashMap`, insertion order to `LinkedHashMap`, sorted keys and ranges to `TreeMap`.

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: These three Maps solve different problems based on ordering needs. HashMap is the go-to for fast lookups when you don't care about iteration order — it gives O of 1 average performance using a hash table. LinkedHashMap extends HashMap and adds a doubly-linked list to maintain insertion order, so iteration comes out in the sequence you put things in. It keeps O of 1 performance but uses a bit more memory for the linked-list pointers. TreeMap is fundamentally different — it uses a red-black tree to keep keys sorted, either by natural order or a custom Comparator. That means O of log n operations, but you get powerful range-query methods through the NavigableMap interface. In practice I'd use HashMap for caching user data by id where order doesn't matter. I'd pick LinkedHashMap for an LRU cache by turning access-order mode on, which moves accessed entries to the end automatically. For TreeMap, picture orders stored by timestamp — you can find all orders between two dates with subMap, no sorting needed. The trap freshers hit is using TreeMap when they don't need sorting, which wastes performance. And remember LinkedHashMap preserves insertion order, it doesn't sort — that's TreeMap's job.

questions.question: How can you implement a simple LRU cache using LinkedHashMap?
questions.title: LRU Cache with LinkedHashMap
questions.direct_answer: Construct a **`LinkedHashMap`** with **`accessOrder=true`**, then override **`removeEldestEntry()`** to return `true` once `size()` exceeds your capacity. The map then auto-evicts the **least recently accessed** entry — a full LRU cache in about ten lines.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of LinkedHashMap's access-order feature and practical application of inheritance to customize collection behavior
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing LinkedHashMap has a three-parameter constructor with accessOrder boolean, or trying to implement LRU from scratch without using this feature
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show the actual concise implementation—it's only a few lines and demonstrates you know this classic Java interview pattern

sections.title: LinkedHashMap's Built-in LRU Support
sections.content:
A **Least Recently Used (LRU) cache** throws out the entry you accessed longest ago once it runs out of room. That keeps the **hot**, frequently used items in memory.

**`LinkedHashMap`** supports this directly. Its three-argument constructor takes a boolean called **`accessOrder`**. Set it to `true`, and every `get` or `put` moves the touched entry to the end of the iteration order. So the **least recently used** entry always sits at the head.

The second piece is **`removeEldestEntry()`** — a `protected` method you **override**. After every `put`, `LinkedHashMap` calls it and asks whether to drop the eldest entry. Return `true` once `size()` passes your capacity, and the map evicts the head entry for you.

Put together, you get a real LRU cache by **subclassing** `LinkedHashMap` in about ten lines. The data structure tracks access order and handles eviction — no separate queue, no manual bookkeeping.

> **Key rule:** the eldest entry is the one at the head of the access order (least recently used), not the oldest by clock time.

sections.title: LinkedHashMap LRU Recipe at a Glance
sections.content:
blue|Step 1|~Enable access order|super(cap, 0.75f, true)|third arg = accessOrder|default false = FIFO
emerald|Step 2|~Override the hook|removeEldestEntry(e)|return size() > capacity|called after every put
violet|How it reorders|~get/put move to tail|most recent at the end|eldest at the head|head is evicted first
amber|Caveat|~Not thread-safe|wrap synchronizedMap|or use Caffeine/Guava|production needs concurrency

sections.title: How Eviction Works After Every Put
sections.content:
Access-order mode plus the `removeEldestEntry` hook evict the head entry automatically. ```mermaid flowchart TD P["put or get a key"] --> M["entry moves to the tail
most recently used"] M --> C{"size greater than capacity?"} C -->|"No"| K["keep all entries"] C -->|"Yes"| E["removeEldestEntry returns true
evict the head entry"] E --> H["head = least recently used"] ``` The head is always the least recently used entry, so eviction needs no manual tracking.

sections.title: Simple LRU Cache with LinkedHashMap
When to Use LinkedHashMap for LRU
sections.content:
Use this approach for a simple **in-memory cache** with bounded size — caching DB query results keyed by query string, or recently accessed user profiles by userId. It's perfect for **single-threaded** code, or when you control synchronization yourself.

It fits lightweight caching of API responses where you want automatic eviction of old data with no cleanup logic. For production **multi-threaded** caches, reach instead for **Caffeine** or **Guava Cache**, which handle concurrency and richer eviction policies for you.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Forgetting the accessOrder parameter:** the two-arg constructor `new LinkedHashMap(capacity, loadFactor)` gives insertion order, so `get` won't reorder and your LRU silently behaves like FIFO.
- **Not overriding removeEldestEntry:** the default always returns `false`, so nothing is ever evicted.
- **Ignoring thread safety:** concurrent `put` or `get` can corrupt the internal linked list, causing `ConcurrentModificationException` or worse.
- **Misreading 'eldest':** the eldest entry is the head of the access order (least recently accessed), not the one with the oldest value.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **`accessOrder=true`** — the third constructor argument enables access-order mode, where `get` and `put` move entries to the tail.
**`removeEldestEntry()`** — a `protected` hook called after every `put`; return `true` to evict the head entry.
**Eldest entry** — the head of the access order (least recently accessed) when access-order mode is on.
**Automatic eviction** — no manual tracking; `LinkedHashMap` reorders and removes for you.
**Single-threaded** — wrap with `Collections.synchronizedMap()` or use `ConcurrentHashMap` for concurrency.
**Production alternative** — Caffeine or Guava Cache give thread-safe LRU with better eviction policies.

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: LinkedHashMap has a special constructor that takes three parameters — capacity, load factor, and a boolean called accessOrder. When you set accessOrder to true, the map tracks access order instead of insertion order. Every get or put on a key moves that entry to the end of the iteration sequence, making it the most recently used. The eldest entry stays at the head. To turn it into an LRU cache, you extend LinkedHashMap and override removeEldestEntry. That method runs after every put with the eldest entry as a parameter. You just return true when the size exceeds your capacity, and LinkedHashMap removes that eldest entry automatically. It's about five or six lines of code. For example, with capacity three, add user one, two, three, then access user one — it moves to the end. Add user four and the cache evicts user two, because it's now least recently used. A pitfall freshers hit is forgetting the accessOrder flag and wondering why their LRU doesn't work — the default is false, which gives insertion order. And this isn't thread-safe, so in production you'd use synchronization or a library like Caffeine.

questions.question: What are the NavigableMap methods in TreeMap and when are they useful?
questions.title: TreeMap NavigableMap Methods
questions.direct_answer: `TreeMap`'s **`NavigableMap`** methods include **`floorKey()`**/**`ceilingKey()`** (nearest key ≤/≥), **`higherKey()`**/**`lowerKey()`** (strictly adjacent), and **`headMap()`**/**`tailMap()`**/**`subMap()`** range views. They make **range queries** and **nearest-neighbor** lookups O(log n) on sorted data.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of TreeMap's sorted capabilities beyond basic put/get operations and knowledge of NavigableMap interface methods
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using TreeMap only for sorted iteration without realizing it provides powerful range query operations that would be expensive with other Maps
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Provide a concrete real-world example like finding events in a time range or stock prices closest to a target value

sections.title: NavigableMap: Beyond Simple Sorted Iteration
sections.content:
A **`TreeMap`** keeps its keys **sorted**, and **`NavigableMap`** is the interface that unlocks what sorting makes possible. `TreeMap` implements it, extending **`SortedMap`** with methods for finding nearby keys and slicing sorted ranges.

The first group is **nearest-key lookups**. **`floorKey(k)`** returns the greatest key less than or equal to `k`; **`ceilingKey(k)`** returns the least key greater than or equal to `k`. **`lowerKey(k)`** and **`higherKey(k)`** do the same but **strictly** — no equality allowed.

The second group is **range views**. **`headMap(k)`** gives every entry below `k`, **`tailMap(k)`** every entry from `k` upward, and **`subMap(from, to)`** the slice in between. These are **live views** backed by the original `TreeMap`, so edits flow both ways.

Every one of these runs in **O(log n)** because the red-black tree is already ordered. Without them you'd scan the whole map at **O(n)**, which defeats the point of paying for a tree.

> **Where it shines:** time-series data, schedules, leaderboards — anywhere you query by range or ask for the nearest key.

sections.title: NavigableMap Methods at a Glance
sections.content:
blue|Nearest (inclusive)|~floor and ceiling|floorKey(k): largest <= k|ceilingKey(k): smallest >= k|null if none qualifies
emerald|Nearest (strict)|~higher and lower|lowerKey(k): largest < k|higherKey(k): smallest > k|excludes equality
violet|Range views|~live, backed views|headMap(k): keys < k|tailMap(k): keys >= k|subMap(from, to): [from, to)
amber|Reverse|~descending order|descendingMap()|descendingKeySet()|no manual sort needed

sections.title: From a Target Key to a Result
sections.content:
Hand `NavigableMap` a target key, and it returns a nearby key or a range slice — always in `O(log n)`. ```mermaid flowchart TD T["target key k"] --> N{"what do you need?"} N -->|"key at or below"| F["floorKey(k)"] N -->|"key at or above"| C["ceilingKey(k)"] N -->|"a range"| S["subMap(from, to)
headMap / tailMap"] F --> O["O(log n) on the red-black tree"] C --> O S --> O ``` Every path stays `O(log n)` because the tree is already sorted.

sections.title: Using NavigableMap for Event Scheduling
When NavigableMap Shines
sections.content:
Use **`floorKey()`/`ceilingKey()`** for the closest match to a target — the stock price at or before a timestamp, or the nearest free appointment slot.

Use **`subMap()`** for **range queries** like all orders between two dates, products in a price band, or log entries inside a time window.

Use **`headMap()`/`tailMap()`** for everything before or after a threshold — events before a deadline, scores above a cutoff. All of these are `O(log n)` versus `O(n)` for filtering a list. A leaderboard can store scores as keys and call `descendingMap()` to walk from highest to lowest.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Iterating to find the nearest key:** looping to find the closest key is `O(n)`; `floorKey()` or `ceilingKey()` does it in `O(log n)` and is the whole reason to use `TreeMap`.
- **Confusing floor/ceiling with higher/lower:** `floorKey` is less-than-or-equal, `lowerKey` is strictly-less-than — mixing them gives off-by-one range boundaries.
- **Modifying range views wrongly:** `subMap()` is a live view; putting an out-of-range key into it throws `IllegalArgumentException`, which surprises freshers expecting a copy.
- **Forgetting descending views:** `descendingMap()` and `descendingKeySet()` give reverse iteration with no manual sorting.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **`NavigableMap`** — extends `SortedMap` with navigation methods for nearest-key and range operations.
**`floorKey(k)` / `ceilingKey(k)`** — greatest key ≤ k, and least key ≥ k; both return null if none qualifies.
**`higherKey(k)` / `lowerKey(k)`** — strictly greater or strictly less than k, for adjacent entries.
**`subMap(from, to)`** — live view of keys in the [from, to) range; changes reflect in both maps.
**`headMap(k)` / `tailMap(k)`** — keys strictly below k, or keys from k upward.
**`descendingMap()`** — a live, reverse-order view of the `TreeMap`, all at `O(log n)`.

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: TreeMap implements the NavigableMap interface, which gives you methods for navigating sorted keys. The most useful are floorKey and ceilingKey for finding the nearest match. FloorKey returns the greatest key less than or equal to your target — the floor of your value. CeilingKey returns the least key greater than or equal — the ceiling. Both are O of log n thanks to the tree. Then higherKey and lowerKey are strictly greater or strictly less, no equality. For range queries you use subMap to get a view of keys between two bounds, headMap for everything before a key, or tailMap for everything after. These are live views backed by the original TreeMap, so a change in one shows up in the other. A concrete example is an event schedule keyed by LocalDateTime. If a user asks what's next after three PM, you call ceilingKey with three PM and get the nearest event at or after that. For all morning events, you call headMap with noon. The common mistake is looping through the whole map to find the nearest key instead of using floorKey or ceilingKey, which wastes TreeMap's sorted structure. And freshers forget subMap views throw IllegalArgumentException if you put a key outside the range — it's a filtered view, not a copy.

questions.question: What are the modern Map methods — getOrDefault(), computeIfAbsent(), and merge()?
questions.title: Modern Map Methods
questions.direct_answer: **`getOrDefault(key, default)`** returns a fallback when the key is missing. **`computeIfAbsent(key, fn)`** lazily computes and stores a value only if the key is absent. **`merge(key, value, fn)`** inserts the value or combines it with the existing one — ideal for frequency counting with `Integer::sum`.

interviewer_intent.testing: Knowledge of Java 8+ Map API enhancements that make common patterns more concise and expressive
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using verbose patterns like checking containsKey() then putting, or getting then null-checking then putting, when these methods do it in one atomic operation
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show the frequency counting pattern with merge() using Integer::sum—it's much cleaner than the old get-increment-put approach

sections.title: Modern Map Methods That Replace Boilerplate
sections.content:
Java 8 added several **default methods** to the **`Map`** interface that wipe out common boilerplate. The three you'll use most are **`getOrDefault`**, **`computeIfAbsent`**, and **`merge`**.

**`getOrDefault(key, fallback)`** is the simplest. It returns the value for a key, or the fallback when the key is missing — no null check, no branch.

**`computeIfAbsent(key, fn)`** builds a value **lazily**. If the key is absent, it runs your function, stores the result, and returns it; if the key is already there, it just returns the existing value. This is the clean way to grow a **`Map` of `List`** without checking for null first.

**`merge(key, value, fn)`** handles **insert-or-update** in one call. Absent key? It stores the value. Present key? It combines the old and new values with your function. The classic use is **frequency counting** with `Integer::sum`.

These methods read as **one map operation each**, where the old style took two or three lookups. They say *what* you want — compute if absent, merge values — instead of *how*.

> **The win:** `map.merge(key, 1, Integer::sum)` counts in one line and one lookup, replacing the old get-check-put dance.

sections.title: Modern Map Methods at a Glance
sections.content:
emerald|getOrDefault|~Safe read|return value or fallback|no null check needed|fallback is eager, keep it cheap
blue|computeIfAbsent|~Lazy get-or-create|runs fn only if absent|stores + returns value|grouping: Map<K,List<V>>
violet|merge|~Insert or combine|absent -> store value|present -> fn(old, new)|counting: merge(k, 1, Integer::sum)
amber|compute|~General update|v is null if absent|handle insert + update|return null removes the key

sections.title: One Intent, One Method
sections.content:
Name what you need, and the method picks itself. ```mermaid flowchart TD N{"what do you need?"} -->|"safe read"| G["getOrDefault
value or fallback"] N -->|"get or create"| C["computeIfAbsent
build only if absent"] N -->|"insert or combine"| M["merge
old + new via function"] M --> F["frequency counting
merge(k, 1, Integer::sum)"] ``` Each modern method maps to a single, clear intent.

sections.title: Practical Uses of Modern Map Methods
When to Use Each Method
sections.content:
Use **`getOrDefault()`** for reading config or cache data that might be missing — you want a sensible fallback, not a null check.

Use **`computeIfAbsent()`** for nested structures like grouping (`Map` of `List`) or caching expensive results — you pay the cost of creating the value only when the key is missing.

Use **`merge()`** for aggregations: frequency counting, summing by category, or combining maps where both new keys and updates matter. The remap function takes old and new, so `Integer::sum` counts, `String::concat` appends, and a lambda handles custom merges.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Manual get-then-null-check-then-put:** writing `if (map.get(key) == null) map.put(key, new ArrayList<>());` instead of `computeIfAbsent(key, k -> new ArrayList<>())`.
- **Eager defaults in getOrDefault():** `getOrDefault(key, expensive())` always runs `expensive()` even when the key exists — use `computeIfAbsent()` for lazy work.
- **Skipping merge for counting:** `put(id, getOrDefault(id, 0) + 1)` is noisier than `merge(id, 1, Integer::sum)`.
- **Confusing computeIfAbsent with putIfAbsent:** `putIfAbsent` stores a pre-computed value, while `computeIfAbsent` computes it lazily only when needed.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **`getOrDefault(key, default)`** — returns the value if present, else the default; no null check needed.
**`computeIfAbsent(key, fn)`** — computes and stores a value only when the key is absent, then returns it.
**`merge(key, value, fn)`** — inserts the value if absent, else combines old and new with the function.
**Lazy evaluation** — `computeIfAbsent` runs its function only when the key is missing, avoiding wasted work.
**Frequency counting** — `merge(key, 1, Integer::sum)` is the idiomatic one-line counter.
**Nested collections** — `computeIfAbsent` shines for `Map` of `List` or `Map` of `Set`, building the inner collection on first access.

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: These are three methods Java 8 added to the Map interface to kill common boilerplate. GetOrDefault is the simplest — you pass a key and a fallback, and if the key isn't there you get the fallback instead of null. Great for config maps with sensible defaults. ComputeIfAbsent takes a key and a mapping function. If the key is absent, it runs the function, stores the value, and returns it; if it's already there, it just returns the existing value without calling the function. That's perfect for lazy initialization of nested collections — a Map of Lists where you want to add an item but the list might not exist yet. Merge is the most powerful for aggregations. It takes a key, a value, and a remap function. Absent key, it inserts the value; present key, it combines old and new with your function. The classic case is frequency counting: merge with the key, the number one, and Integer colon colon sum increments the count or starts it at one, all in one line. Before Java 8 you'd get the count, null-check it, then put — far more verbose. A common mistake is calling getOrDefault with an expensive default, which always runs even when the key exists. Use computeIfAbsent for expensive work because it's lazy.

beats.text: These are default methods on the Map interface. getOrDefault returns a fallback when a key is missing. computeIfAbsent builds and stores a value only when the key's absent. merge inserts a value, or combines it with the one already there.
The old patterns made two or three lookups. Check containsKey, then get, then put. That's wasteful and noisy. The new methods do the check and the change in one call.

items: getOrDefault takes a key and a fallback, and hands back the fallback when the key's missing.
computeIfAbsent builds the value only when it's absent. Perfect for a Map of lists.
merge with one and Integer sum counts occurrences in a single line.
compute handles insert and update together, since the value's null when the key is absent.

beats.text: Picture a product catalog counting views per product. merge with the id and Integer sum bumps the count or starts it at one. Here's the non-obvious part. That merge is one map lookup, not two. The old getOrDefault-then-put version reads the map twice. So merge wins on clarity and speed.

items: computeIfAbsent returns the existing or new value. It's a one-step get-or-create, not just a conditional put.
merge with a function that returns null drops the key. Watch that when your combiner can return null.

speakable_v2.cap: So merge counts, computeIfAbsent groups, and getOrDefault reads safely. Three methods cover most Java 8 Map questions.
